title: Heterogeneous GPU pools Terraform module with safeguarded autoscaler (ASG/Karpenter) for Private VPC
creator: Maya Chen
description: Build a reusable Terraform module (and lightweight submodules) to provision heterogeneous GPU node pools inside Private VPC deployments with support for two autoscaling backends: ASG-based autoscaling (AWS ASG + mixed instances) and Karpenter-based provisioning. The module must: 1) support multiple GPU instance classes (e.g., a100, h100, t4) behind named pools, 2) allow configuration of on-demand vs spot allocation with safe spot fallback rules, 3) expose fine-grained healthcheck and drain policies (kubelet + driver health + custom Prometheus probe), 4) integrate with Private networking constraints (subnet selection, ENI limits, security groups) and 5) provide upgrade/rollout primitives (canary pool, maxUnavailable, create_before_destroy semantics) so runtime upgrades and driver updates are safe for production workloads. The outcome should be a single public module interface that teams can pin to via source/version and an internal example usage manifest for Private staging and production accounts.
acceptance_criteria: Terraform module can create at least two named GPU pools (high-memory A100 and cost-optimized T4) in Private VPC using the same interface
Autoscaling switch (provider = "asg" | "karpenter") toggles the created resources and policies; both modes tested end-to-end in staging
Spot pools gracefully fall back to on-demand after configurable grace period without pod eviction storms
Healthchecks detect NV driver failures and trigger node cordon+drain with retries; healthcheck metrics visible in staging Grafana dashboard
Upgrade path: example plan for driver upgrade uses canary pool, verifies application-level SLOs for 30 minutes before full rollout
Module has unit tests (terraform-compliance / kitchen-terraform style) and an automated pipeline that runs plan/apply in an isolated sandbox; docs and example manifests added to Confluence.
design_decisions: Choice: single top-level module with two submodules (asgs/karpenter). Rationale: keep consumer interface stable while allowing clustering differences to live in submodules
Use "create_before_destroy" lifecycle and instance refresh where supported to reduce downtime during node type changes; trade-off: temporary double-capacity during upgrades

Spot fallback: implement a controller that updates Karpenter provisioner tags or ASG capacity policy to shift workload to on-demand when spot eviction rate > threshold. Rationale: fewer sudden OOMs vs relying on cloud spot notifications alone
Healthchecks: combine kubelet node conditions + nvtop/driver-exporter heartbeat + node-exporter filesystem checks. Rationale: detect both OS/driver and hardware failures
IAM: module will create minimal IAM roles/policies but allow consumers to pass existing roles to satisfy enterprise constraints
Telemetry: emit node-pool labels and autoscaler decisions to Prometheus via node-exporter + custom exporter for easier cost attribution
risk_mitigation: Canary-first rollout: default to creating a small canary pool in same AZ; only scale to full capacity after smoke tests pass
Automated rollback: Terraform plans for upgrades will include a validation step that checks Pod readiness and tail latencies; pipeline blocks on regressions
Quota checks: module preflight will calculate likely vCPU/GPU quotas and fail fast with actionable message
Driver package pinning: don't auto-upgrade drivers — require explicit version bump in module inputs to avoid silent breakage
implementation_notes: Submodules: modules/karpenter-provisioner, modules/asg-mixed-instance, modules/networking (ENI & SG glue)
Expose inputs: instance_types (list), gpu_driver_package (string), spot_percentage (number), min_size/max_size, scale_down_delay_seconds
Outputs: node_pool_name, provisioner_name, autoscaler_policy_id, kube_taints, generated_user_data_hash
Use provider-agnostic naming for resources and tag with redwood:private-pool to simplify cleanup scripts
Testing: create terraform sandbox account with mock workloads (tf-job and batch generation) to validate burst patterns
